plain_english: Some people hear that you should be firm in your decisions and that your will is free and can't be forced. They hear that everything else can be blocked, enslaved, or controlled by others. So they think they should stick to every decision they make, no matter what. But first, the decision needs to be a good one. I want you to have strength in your body — but the kind that comes from being healthy and fit. If I can see you have the strength of a crazy person and you're proud of it, I'll tell you: "Go see a doctor. That's not real strength. That's weakness."
original_excerpt: When some persons have heard these words, that a man ought to be constant (firm), and that the will is naturally free and not subject to compulsion, but that all other things are subject to hindrance, to slavery, and are in the power of others, they suppose that they ought without deviation to abide by everything which they have determined. But in the first place that which has been determined ought to be sound (true). I require tone (sinews) in the body, but such as exists in a healthy body, in an athletic body; but if it is plain to me that you have the tone of a frenzied man and you boast of it, I shall say to you, Man, seek the physician; this is not tone, but atony (deficiency in right tone).
source_reference: Discourses, To or Against Those Who Obstinately Persist in What They Have Determined, Section 1

plain_english: Something similar happens to people who listen to these teachings the wrong way. This happened to one of my friends. For no good reason, he decided to starve himself to death. I heard about it on the third day after he stopped eating. I went to ask him what was going on. "I've made up my mind," he said. "But tell me what made you decide this. If you decided for the right reasons, we'll sit with you and help you die. But if your decision is unreasonable, change your mind." "We should stick to our decisions." "What are you doing, man? We should stick to our decisions only when they're right. If you're convinced this is right, then don't change your mind. Keep going and say, 'We should stick to our decisions.'"
original_excerpt: In a different way something of the same kind is felt by those who listen to these discourses in a wrong manner; which was the case with one of my companions, who for no reason resolved to starve himself to death. I heard of it when it was the third day of his abstinence from food, and I went to inquire what had happened. "I have resolved," he said. "But still tell me what it was which induced you to resolve; for if you have resolved rightly, we shall sit with you and assist you to depart, but if you have made an unreasonable resolution, change your mind." "We ought to keep to our determinations." "What are you doing, man? We ought to keep not to all our determinations, but to those which are right; for if you are now persuaded that it is right, do not change your mind, if you think fit, but persist and say, We ought to abide by our determinations.
source_reference: Discourses, To or Against Those Who Obstinately Persist in What They Have Determined, Section 1

plain_english: Won't you start by examining whether your decision is sound or not? Then build on that solid foundation. But if you lay a rotten foundation, won't your pathetic little building collapse even faster when you pile more materials on top? For no good reason, you want to remove from life a man who is your friend and companion, a fellow citizen of both our city and the greater human city. While you're committing murder and destroying an innocent man, do you say you should stick to your decisions? And if it ever crossed your mind to kill me, should you stick to that decision too?
original_excerpt: Will you not make the beginning and lay the foundation in an inquiry whether the determination is sound or not sound, and so then build on it firmness and security? But if you lay a rotten and ruinous foundation, will not your miserable little building fall down the sooner, the more and the stronger are the materials which you shall lay on it? Without any reason would you withdraw from us out of life a man who is a friend and a companion, a citizen of the same city, both the great and the small city? Then while you are committing murder and destroying a man who has done no wrong, do you say that you ought to abide by your determinations? And if it ever in any way came into your head to kill me, ought you to abide by your determinations?"
source_reference: Discourses, To or Against Those Who Obstinately Persist in What They Have Determined, Section 1

plain_english: This man was hard to convince. But some people today? Impossible. Now I understand that old saying: "You can't persuade a fool, and you can't force them either." God help me if I ever have a stubborn fool for a friend. Nothing is harder to deal with. "I've made up my mind," he says. So have crazy people. But the crazier their beliefs about things that don't exist, the more medicine they need. Why don't you act like a sick person and call a doctor? "I'm sick, teacher. Help me. Tell me what to do. I'll listen to you." That's how it should work here too: "I don't know what I should do, but I came here to learn." But no. Instead it's: "Talk to me about other things. On this topic, I've already decided." What other things?
original_excerpt: Now this man was with difficulty persuaded to change his mind. But it is impossible to convince some persons at present; so that I seem now to know what I did not know before, the meaning of the common saying, that you can neither persuade nor break a fool. May it never be my lot to have a wise fool for my friend; nothing is more untractable. "I am determined," the man says. Madmen are also, but the more firmly they form a judgment on things which do not exist, the more hellebore they require. Will you not act like a sick man and call in the physician?—I am sick, master, help me; consider what I must do: it is my duty to obey you. So it is here also: I know not what I ought to do, but I am come to learn.—Not so; but speak to me about other things: upon this I have determined.—What other things?
source_reference: Discourses, To or Against Those Who Obstinately Persist in What They Have Determined, Section 1

plain_english: What's more important than convincing yourself that it's not enough to just make a decision and stick to it? This kind of rigid energy is madness, not health. "I'll die before you make me do this!" Why, man? What happened? "I've made up my mind." Lucky for me you haven't decided to kill me! "I won't take any money." Why not? "I've made up my mind." Know this: with the same stubborn energy you use to refuse money now, nothing stops you from later wanting to take it for no good reason and saying "I've made up my mind." Like a sick body where fluids shift from one part to another, a sick soul doesn't know which way to lean. But when you add stubborn determination to this back-and-forth, the problem becomes impossible to fix.
original_excerpt: for what is greater and more useful than for you to be persuaded that it is not sufficient to have made your determination and not to change it. This is the tone (energy) of madness, not of health.—I will die, if you compel me to this.—Why, man? What has happened?—I have determined—I have had a lucky escape that you have not determined to kill me—I take no money. Why?—I have determined—Be assured that with the very tone (energy) which you now use in refusing to take, there is nothing to hinder you at some time from inclining without reason to take money, and then saying, I have determined. As in a distempered body, subject to defluxions, the humor inclines sometimes to these parts, and then to those, so too a sickly soul knows not which way to incline; but if to this inclination and movement there is added a tone (obstinate resolution), then the evil becomes past help and cure.
source_reference: Discourses, To or Against Those Who Obstinately Persist in What They Have Determined, Section 1
